segments.body: Cardellini also looks back on Freaks and Geeks, cancelled before its first season had finished airing but later embraced as a lasting television favourite. After winning her first Emmy for DTF St Louis, she says she enjoys changing direction rather than committing to a “scream queen” identity.

content.headline: Aberfan survivors recall the long fight for justice in new documentary
content.shortHeadline: Aberfan’s families and their decades-long fight
content.standfirst: The documentary revisits the 1966 disaster and the failures that followed it, through the memories of survivors and bereaved families. Its review finds the treatment of the village by officials as distressing as the tragedy itself.

image.caption: The aftermath of the Aberfan disaster in 1966.

sources.originalTitle: Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back review – the contempt they have faced to get justice is sickening

segments.body: On 21 October 1966, a spoil tip engulfed a school and homes in Aberfan, killing 116 children and 28 adults. Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back begins with survivors’ and families’ memories before tracing the campaign to hold the National Coal Board and government to account.

segments.title: A second injury
segments.body: The documentary recounts how the inquiry blamed the Coal Board, yet no one was personally punished. Families also faced years of resistance over liability and the removal of the tips; the board demanded money from the disaster fund to pay for the work. The review highlights the village’s organising and the later return of the fund money by the Blair government.

content.headline: Seven shows to stream this week, from The Audacity to Lupin
content.shortHeadline: Seven shows to stream this week
content.standfirst: A new comedy about wealthy tech executives leads this week’s picks, alongside a killer-gnome series, a grooming documentary and new seasons of familiar streaming favourites.

image.caption: Billy Magnussen and Sarah Goldberg in The Audacity.

sources.originalTitle: The Audacity to Nobody Wants This: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Audacity, from Succession writer Jonathan Glatzer, sends up a rich, morally compromised tech CEO and the world around him. The guide says the comedy does not quite reach Succession’s heights, but finds plenty of bite in its portrait of people insulated by wealth.

segments.title: Other picks this week
segments.body: The week’s recommendations range from Australian horror-comedy Gnomes and a documentary about the online grooming and murder of Breck Bednar to returning series Nobody Wants This and Lupin. The selection also includes a Halloween edition of Last One Laughing and a three-part investigation into police access to the encrypted Sky ECC app.

content.headline: Tonight on TV: a ketamine documentary and rare Only Fools and Horses clips
content.shortHeadline: Tonight: ketamine, Only Fools and more
content.standfirst: Stacey Dooley meets long-term ketamine users, while Only Fools and Horses fans get a look at deleted scenes. The evening’s other picks include a family documentary and a Bafta-nominated film about addiction.

image.caption: Stacey Dooley in Down the K-Hole.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: Stacey Dooley learns about ‘ket bladder’

segments.body: Down the K-Hole follows Stacey Dooley as she speaks with long-term ketamine users about the effects of the drug, including bladder damage and the appeal of dissociation. The programme is presented as an eye-opening account of consequences, not as a first-hand investigation by Dooley into her own use.

segments.title: Other evening choices
segments.body: The schedule also offers previously unseen Only Fools and Horses clips, a documentary about a mother and daughter navigating addiction and estrangement, and a programme about novelist John le Carré. The guide rounds out its picks with baking, police drama and live sport.

content.headline: Time’s young offender institute drama shows how anger is reinforced
content.shortHeadline: Time examines anger inside a young offenders’ institute
content.standfirst: The third series of Jimmy McGovern’s prison drama follows boys held in near-isolation and the adults responsible for them. Its review finds a devastating account of violence, emotional need and a system that leaves little room for change.

image.caption: David Tennant and Louis McCartney in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time review – David Tennant’s furious drama is as important as Adolescence

segments.body: The final series of Time moves into a young offender institution where boys can be locked in their cells for 23 hours a day under a “keep apart” system. David Tennant plays a weary but not entirely unfeeling officer; Siobhan Finneran returns as a chaplain who has lost her faith but continues to work with the inmates.

perspectives.body: The review argues the series should receive the national attention given to Adolescence, while acknowledging that the prison system’s complexity and the bleakness of its subject may make that harder.

segments.title: What the drama makes visible
segments.body: The boys’ histories include serious violence, but the series also shows grief, abuse and a lack of language for emotion feeding further harm. The review praises the young cast and argues that the drama’s account of isolation and pent-up anger makes the realities of young offender institutions difficult to ignore.

content.headline: Sarah Solemani’s The Party brings class, grief and ambition to television
content.shortHeadline: Sarah Solemani on class, grief and The Party
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and showrunner discusses adapting Elizabeth Day’s novel into a drama about a journalist and a Tory politician, and how personal loss and class have shaped her work.

image.caption: Actor, writer and showrunner Sarah Solemani.

sources.originalTitle: Sarah Solemani: ‘I performed at my mum’s hospice bed two weeks before she died’

segments.body: Sarah Solemani stars in and runs The Party, adapted from Elizabeth Day’s novel. The drama follows a working-class journalist and a Conservative politician whose old friendship hides a secret. Solemani says she has long tried to bring stories about the British class system to television without being forced to treat class as a genre in itself.

segments.title: Writing from experience
segments.body: Solemani speaks about losing her mother at 16, the urgency that followed, and her view that creativity requires a willingness to be emotionally exposed. She also says the #MeToo movement changed working conditions on sets, describing a marked difference from her experience as a young actor.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic expedition into a strange, critical odyssey
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony is a strange Antarctic odyssey
content.standfirst: This exploration game sends a penguin through a world of Nazis, Lovecraftian horrors and scattered words. Its fractured storytelling becomes a critique of the human urge to conquer and plunder.

image.caption: A penguin explores the Antarctic world of Penguin Colony.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: Penguin Colony casts the player as a penguin exploring an Antarctic landscape where Nazis pursue an ancient entity. Words replace the usual treasure as collectibles, and hopping between different penguin species changes how the player moves through the terrain.

segments.title: A history seen from another angle
segments.body: The review praises the game’s unsettling shifts between low-poly exploration, narrated expedition history and archive footage. Its eventual critique of Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism is tied to a wider invitation to experience the world without treating it as something to conquer, though technical glitches occasionally interrupt the play.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time remake makes a classic feel new under the thumbs
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time gets a striking Switch 2 remake
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s remake updates movement, camera and sound for Switch 2 while preserving the game’s familiar world and puzzles. Link’s new look is divisive, but the preview finds a coherent reimagining in motion.

image.caption: Link in Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: The Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time gives Link a sprint, manual jump, free-rotating camera and a streamlined inventory. Familiar dungeons and puzzles remain, but the upgraded controls make the 1998 game feel markedly different to play.

perspectives.body: The preview sees Link’s glossy, wide-eyed redesign as a point of debate, but suggests its doll-like look may reflect a Japanese puppet-theatre tradition rather than a simple pursuit of 4K detail.

segments.title: The challenge of revisiting a classic
segments.body: The remake’s enhanced environments and newly orchestrated soundtrack help refresh the familiar adventure, though the reviewer questions whether Hyrule Field can recreate the freedom players felt in 1998. The more traditional dungeon structure may itself be part of the appeal for returning fans.

content.headline: Could a new wave of independent arcades bring gaming back to the high street?
content.shortHeadline: Independent arcades could bring gaming back to the high street
content.standfirst: After years of sprawling games designed to occupy players indefinitely, interest is growing in shorter experiences and social play. The case for independent arcades is less about nostalgia than shared discovery.

image.caption: Players return to the social experience of arcade gaming.

sources.originalTitle: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth

segments.body: The article argues that publishers’ pursuit of “forever games” has helped renew interest in shorter, more focused experiences. New arcade-minded titles and specialist venues suggest a possible return to gaming spaces where players can try different games without committing all their time to one.

segments.title: A local place for players
segments.body: Rather than simply reproducing retro bars, the model proposed is closer to an independent bookshop or record store: a curated collection, knowledgeable staff and events that help build a community. Arcade specialist Will Freeman sees small venues opening on that basis, though he cautions that the current signs do not amount to a boom.

perspectives.body: Freeman says gaming bars and cafés show that out-of-home gaming can be sustainable, but describes independent arcades as a handful of emerging projects rather than a boom.

content.headline: A £350 GTA collector’s box reflects gaming’s growing price barrier
content.shortHeadline: The £350 GTA box reflects gaming’s rising costs
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI merchandise box does not include the game itself. The article sees its price as part of a wider shift that risks making console and PC gaming feel like a luxury hobby.

image.caption: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI collector’s box.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s £350 Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection contains merchandise but no copy or download code for the game. With the game priced separately at £70, buying both would cost £420.

segments.title: Who can afford to play?
segments.body: The writer argues that expensive collector’s editions fit a broader pattern of rising console and game prices, as publishers pursue a smaller group of high-spending customers. Mobile games remain widely accessible, but the console and PC experiences that form the article’s focus are increasingly difficult to access without substantial spending.

content.headline: Ngumoha inspires Liverpool's seven-goal comeback win over Villarreal
content.shortHeadline: Ngumoha sparks Liverpool comeback against Villarreal
content.standfirst: The 18-year-old helped turn a two-goal deficit into a 4-3 Champions League win, setting up two goals and earning the player-of-the-match award. His fearless display also made history for Liverpool.

image.caption: Rio Ngumoha, who became Liverpool's youngest player to score or assist in the Champions League.

sources.originalTitle: The night 'ruthless' Ngumoha came of age for Liverpool

segments.body: Liverpool trailed Villarreal by two goals before Alexis Mac Allister pulled one back. Rio Ngumoha then supplied the cross for Ronald Araujo's equaliser and, after the break, set up Mac Allister to put Liverpool ahead. Florian Wirtz added a fourth in the 4-3 win.

segments.title: A landmark performance
segments.body: At 18 years and 52 days, Ngumoha became the youngest Liverpool player to score or assist for the club in the Champions League. He completed seven of eight dribbles and had 12 touches in the opposition box. Head coach Andoni Iraola praised his attitude, while stressing that the teenager is still developing.

content.headline: Foden scores a hat-trick as Manchester City beat AEK Athens 5-1
content.shortHeadline: Foden's hat-trick leads City's 5-1 Champions League win
content.standfirst: Phil Foden had a hand in four goals as City pulled clear after AEK briefly made it 2-1. His performance offered a timely reminder of his scoring ability and gave Enzo Maresca a look at him in a central role.

image.caption: Phil Foden, who scored a hat-trick and provided an assist against AEK Athens.

sources.originalTitle: No Haaland, no problem - can Foden be Man City's alternative goalscorer?

segments.body: Foden scored three times and assisted another goal in City's 5-1 win over AEK Athens. His second strike was a first-time finish into the top corner. It was his first Premier League goal in 10 months at the weekend, followed by a Champions League hat-trick that he said was good for his confidence.

segments.title: A possible option up front
segments.body: Erling Haaland was named in the squad but rested after taking a blow to his foot in the previous game. Foden started on the right before moving into a false-nine role, which he said he enjoyed. Manager Enzo Maresca said he considers Foden one of England's best players and expects him to help the team.

content.headline: Pakistan's Arafat Minhas takes six as England collapse in ODI opener
content.shortHeadline: Arafat's six wickets send England to defeat by Pakistan
content.standfirst: England were bowled out for 215 chasing Pakistan's 302-9, losing their last seven wickets for 50 runs. Arafat Minhas made 59 and took 6-40 as England began their winter with a heavy defeat.

image.caption: Pakistan's Arafat Minhas, who made 59 and took 6-40 against England.

sources.originalTitle: Sloppy England start winter with Pakistan defeat

segments.body: Arafat Minhas made 59 after being dropped on 12, helping Pakistan reach 302-9. He then took six wickets as England's chase fell apart: after a 91-run opening stand, England lost seven wickets for 50 and finished on 215. Tom Banton top-scored for England with 57.

segments.title: A test for England's World Cup build-up
segments.body: England captain Harry Brook said his side had expected to chase the target but lost too many wickets in clumps and needed to put the spinners under more pressure. This was the first of a potential 21 ODIs before next year's World Cup; England were also without Jos Buttler, Jofra Archer and Jacob Bethell.

content.headline: Mark Allen considers retirement after Northern Ireland Open defeat
content.shortHeadline: Allen says retirement is on his mind after Belfast exit
content.standfirst: The former world number one lost 4-2 to Jordan Brown on his return to competition and said retirement is something he has been considering. Allen has not made a decision, but says something must change before the UK Championship.

image.caption: Mark Allen after his Northern Ireland Open defeat, as he considers his future in snooker.

sources.originalTitle: Allen considers retirement after NI Open exit

segments.body: Allen said simply “Yeah” when asked if he was considering retirement after losing 4-2 to fellow Antrim player Jordan Brown in the Northern Ireland Open first round. He said playing the match was an achievement after a difficult period and that he had wanted his last match, if it came to that, to be in Belfast.

segments.title: No decision yet
segments.body: Allen said he would not announce retirement immediately after a defeat, but that something needed to change within six weeks for him to return for the UK Championship. The 40-year-old has won 12 ranking tournaments. Brown said he hoped Allen would continue, while acknowledging his own difficult circumstances.

content.headline: Swiatek ends her season after thigh injury and misses WTA Finals
content.shortHeadline: Swiatek ends a difficult season early
content.standfirst: The six-time Grand Slam champion has withdrawn from Ningbo with a thigh injury and will not qualify for the WTA Finals. She says she needs a longer period to rest and recover before returning in 2027.

image.caption: Iga Swiatek, whose 2026 season ends after a thigh injury.

sources.originalTitle: Swiatek ends 'most demanding' season of career

segments.body: Iga Swiatek has ended her 2026 season after withdrawing from the Ningbo Open with a thigh injury. The world number nine will miss the WTA Finals for the first time since 2019. She said the past few months, and years, had been intense and that she needed to recover fully.

segments.title: A season of change
segments.body: Swiatek ends the year with one title, the Canadian Open, and a 42-16 win-loss record. She did not reach a Grand Slam quarter-final in 2026, and her latest major title was Wimbledon last year. After changing coaches in March, she said she was proud of her work and progress in the second half of the season.

content.headline: Bavuma's 179 gives South Africa a chance to fight back against Australia
content.shortHeadline: Bavuma's 179 revives South Africa against Australia
content.standfirst: Temba Bavuma batted through South Africa's recovery from 110-6 to make his highest Test score and help his side declare. Kagiso Rabada then struck in Australia's reply, leaving the hosts with a chance to revive the series.

image.caption: Temba Bavuma, whose 179 was his highest Test score.

sources.originalTitle: Bavuma epic drags SA back into Test - have they time to beat Australia?

segments.body: South Africa captain Temba Bavuma made 179, his highest Test score, after arriving at the crease with his side 12-2 on day one. He shared a 183-run eighth-wicket partnership with Simon Harmer and helped South Africa recover from 110-6 before declaring on 425-9.

segments.title: A chance, but no result yet
segments.body: Rabada dismissed Australia opener Nic Maddinson in the first over of the reply, but poor light soon stopped play. Bavuma said the innings had given South Africa a chance, while acknowledging that an earlier declaration might have allowed more overs in favourable conditions. The Test was still in progress in the report.

content.headline: Champions League goals record raises questions about entertainment and jeopardy
content.shortHeadline: Champions League goals surge sets a new record
content.standfirst: This season's competition is averaging 4.16 goals a game, its highest rate in Champions League history. The scoring surge is drawing praise for the entertainment, as well as questions about what the expanded format means for jeopardy.

image.caption: Phil Foden, who scored a hat-trick in Manchester City's 5-1 win over AEK Athens.

sources.originalTitle: No jeopardy but loads of fun - Champions League sets new goals record

segments.body: The Champions League has produced 187 goals at an average of 4.16 per game, the highest rate in its history. Forty goals were scored across Tuesday's nine matches. Last week's two matchdays produced 78 goals, the highest-scoring matchday total since the league phase began.

segments.title: More goals, but what do they mean?
segments.body: The 36-team league phase replaced groups of four with eight matches for each side. Some argue that the format gives teams room to play more expansively because a defeat early on is less costly. Times football writer Tom Arnott told BBC Radio 5 Live that the games are thrilling, but questioned whether the reduced jeopardy makes the results feel less meaningful.

content.headline: Jake Smith's story highlights the risks of under-fuelling in sport
content.shortHeadline: Runner Jake Smith explains the danger of REDs
content.standfirst: British runner Jake Smith says he was diagnosed with relative energy deficiency in sport after repeated injuries and under-fuelling. Experts and athletes explain how REDs can affect men as well as women, and why it may go unnoticed.

sources.originalTitle: Race, illness, injury, repeat - REDs and why men are suffering in silence

segments.body: Jake Smith says he suffered two stress fractures in four months before being diagnosed with relative energy deficiency in sport, or REDs. The condition can result from insufficient energy intake and may cause injuries, fatigue, disrupted sleep and longer-term health problems if left untreated.

segments.title: Why it can be missed
segments.body: The report says REDs can be harder to recognise in men, where symptoms such as falling testosterone and fatigue may be less obvious. Triathlete Jonny Brownlee described under-fuelling as a contributor to injuries in his career; experts say the condition is reversible, but warn that athletes may mistake it for burnout or fail to match their food intake to training demands.
